title: My Safe Florida Condo: how the state's storm-hardening grant works, and where the program stands now
seoTitle: My Safe Florida Condo Grant: How It Works in Florida
description: Florida's My Safe Florida Condo pilot offers a 2-to-1 state match for storm hardening. Here is who qualifies, the 75% owner vote, and where it stands now.
dek: The state will put up $2 for every $1 a condo association spends on windows, doors and roofs, up to $175,000. But the money is limited, the rules are strict, and a 2026 bill to change them did not become law.

body.text: Many condo owners have heard about My Safe Florida Home, the state program that helps single-family homeowners pay for hurricane upgrades. Fewer know there is a separate program for condo buildings: the My Safe Florida Condominium Pilot Program, often called My Safe Florida Condo.

It can pay for a big share of new windows, doors or roof work. But it has strict rules, a hard cap and limited money. Here is what the 2026 Florida Statutes say, and what the state’s own page says today. It is a guide, not legal advice.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: DFS: the Florida Department of Financial Services, which runs the program. Pilot program: a trial program that runs only as long as the Legislature funds it. Opening protection: protecting the openings in a building, meaning exterior doors, garage doors, windows and skylights. Mitigation: work that makes a building less likely to be damaged by a hurricane. Total voting interests: all the votes in the association, usually one per unit, counting every unit, not just the owners who show up. Milestone inspection: the structural inspection Florida requires for condo buildings three stories or taller as they age. SIRS: the structural integrity reserve study, which sets how much the association must save for the building's major parts.
What the program is

Section 215.55871 of Florida law creates the pilot inside DFS. It has two parts. First, a licensed inspector looks at the building and writes a report. Second, the association can apply for a grant to make the upgrades the report recommends.

The law is clear that this is not a promise of money. It says the section "does not create an entitlement" for associations or owners, and that the program is "subject to annual legislative appropriations." In other words, it runs only when the Legislature sets aside money for it.
Who can qualify
Under the 2026 statute, these are the main rules:

items: Location: the property must be in the "service area," which the law defines as the area 15 miles inward of a coastline.
Building size: the building must be three or more stories tall. A building that gets a grant must contain at least two homes. Detached units on their own lots don't count.
Safety paperwork first: the association cannot apply unless it has complied with the state's milestone inspection and SIRS requirements.

Windows: for a window or other opening-protection grant, the windows must be common elements under the condo's declaration, the document that created the condominium. Common elements are the parts of the property the association owns and maintains for everyone.
One application per property, signed by the board president under penalty of perjury.

body.text: The votes: a board vote, then 75% of resident owners
To join the pilot, the association needs a majority vote of the board or a majority of the total voting interests.

If the grant would improve units, the bar is much higher. The law requires approval by "at least 75 percent of all unit owners who reside within the structure or building" getting the grant. Each of those owners must also sign an acknowledged statement that goes with the application. For a building with many absentee or seasonal owners, reaching that number can take real legwork.

Before owners vote, the association must give every owner a disclosure form created by DFS, signed by the board president and treasurer. The vote can happen at the annual budget meeting or at an owner meeting called for it. Within 14 days after a yes vote, the association must send written notice of the decision to all owners.
What the money pays for, and how much

The inspection report must list recommended improvements, a range of cost estimates, and estimated insurance premium discounts. DFS's program page says the initial inspection is free and done by a program-contracted inspector. An association can get the inspection without applying for a grant.

Grants can pay for exterior doors, garage doors, windows and skylights, and for roof work: stronger roof-to-wall connections, better roof-deck attachment, a secondary water barrier, and a new roof covering. Water intrusion devices are also allowed. The work must earn a mitigation credit or discount on the building's insurance rate. If that credit requires protecting every opening, DFS must require all of them to be done.

The match is $1 from the association for every $2 from the state, based on the real cost of the project. The total state grant cannot be more than $175,000 per association. DFS's page says these are reimbursement grants: the association pays first and is paid back after the work passes a final inspection. The grant must be approved before work starts.

Here is a quick example. On a $90,000 window project, the association would pay $30,000 and the state $60,000. At the cap, a $262,500 project would get the full $175,000, and anything above that is the association's to pay.

The association chooses its own contractors, but each must be licensed and pull the required permits, and DFS checks their licenses before approving a grant. Once a grant is approved, the association has one year to finish construction and ask for a final inspection, or ask for more time. Otherwise the application is treated as abandoned and the money goes back to DFS.
Where the program stands

The Legislature put $30 million into the pilot in 2024, with $27,636,000 of it for grants, according to a 2026 Florida Senate staff analysis. DFS opened the program on November 13, 2024, and announced on November 20, 2024, that it had already received the maximum number of applications for the money available.

In 2026, the Senate voted 37–0 on March 4 for SB 1706, which would have changed who qualifies. Its House companion, HB 1497, died in a House subcommittee on March 13, and the Senate bill's last action shows it waiting in the House. So those changes did not become law, and the 2026 statute keeps the rules above.

Today, DFS's program page says it now handles all inspection and grant applications by email. The page lists no deadlines and does not say how much money is left or whether new grant applications are being taken. The law also says DFS may not accept grant applications or keep a waiting list once the money is fully committed, unless the Legislature says otherwise. The only sure way to know is to ask the program directly: condopilot@myfloridacfo.com or (850) 413-2971.
What to do
If you are an owner:

items: Ask your board or manager in writing: "Has our association applied to My Safe Florida Condo, and where does that application stand?"
If a vote is coming, read the DFS disclosure form before the meeting. If the grant would touch your unit, your signature may be one of the 75% the building needs.
Ask what the association's one-third share would cost and how it would be paid, since the state pays back only after the work is done.

body.text: If you are a board member:

items: Contact the program first to ask whether it is taking new inspection and grant applications, and get the answer in writing.
Pull your declaration and check whether windows are common elements. Ask the association attorney if it is unclear.
Make sure your milestone inspection and SIRS paperwork is in order; the law makes it a condition of applying.
Plan the cash: the association pays its contractors first, and the project has a one-year clock once the grant is approved.
Keep the signed disclosure form and the meeting minutes in the official records, as the law requires.

faq.q: Is My Safe Florida Condo still accepting applications?
faq.a: DFS's program page does not say whether new grant applications are being taken or how much money is left. It says applications are now handled by email. The program closed to new applications days after it opened in November 2024 because demand exceeded the money. Ask the program at condopilot@myfloridacfo.com or (850) 413-2971.

faq.q: How much does My Safe Florida Condo pay?
faq.a: The state pays $2 for every $1 the association spends on the actual project cost, up to $175,000 per association. DFS says it is a reimbursement grant, so the association pays first and is paid back after a final inspection.

faq.q: Can I apply for My Safe Florida Condo for my own condo unit?
faq.a: No. Under section 215.55871 of Florida law, an owner may benefit through a grant awarded to the association but may not take part in the pilot individually. The association applies.

faq.q: What vote is needed for a My Safe Florida Condo grant?
faq.a: The association needs a majority vote of the board or of the total voting interests to join. If the grant improves units, it also needs approval from at least 75 percent of all unit owners who live in the building getting the grant.

faq.q: Which condo buildings qualify for My Safe Florida Condo?
faq.a: Buildings three or more stories tall, with at least two homes, within 15 miles of a coastline, whose association has complied with Florida's milestone inspection and SIRS requirements. For window grants, the windows must be common elements under the declaration.
